notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Moses to give him directions for ordaining the priests. Now that the tabernacle was finished and the sacrificial laws were given, God called Aaron and his sons to begin their service. God alone chooses who may approach Him in holy ministry.

God told Moses to gather Aaron, his sons, their priestly garments, the anointing oil, and all the required offerings at the tabernacle entrance. He also commanded the leaders representing the whole congregation to assemble there. To consecrate means to set someone or something apart for God's holy purpose. Holding this ceremony before the whole assembly showed everyone that God had chosen these men.

Moses did exactly what the Lord commanded and gathered Israel's leaders at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. He declared to the people that this ceremony was God's direct command, not his own personal idea. True worship and service must always rest on what God has commanded.

Moses brought Aaron and his sons forward and washed their entire bodies with water. Although they might have looked clean outwardly, this washing showed they needed inner spiritual cleansing before serving the Lord. God requires all who draw near to Him to be cleansed from sin.

Moses dressed Aaron in the high priest's inner tunic, tied the sash around him, put on the blue robe, and placed the ephod over it. He then fastened the woven band around Aaron to keep the garments securely in place. These beautiful vestments showed the dignity of Aaron's sacred office.

Moses fastened the breastpiece over Aaron's chest and placed the Urim and Thummim inside it. The Urim and Thummim were sacred objects used by the high priest to determine God's will for the nation. This reminded Aaron that his duty was to seek God's guidance and carry the people upon his heart.

Moses placed the linen turban on Aaron's head and attached a plate of pure gold to the front. This golden crown was engraved with the words 'Holiness to the Lord.' It constantly reminded the priest and the people that his entire life belonged to God.

Moses took the sacred anointing oil and rubbed it on the tabernacle and everything inside it. Anointing means putting holy oil on someone or something to dedicate it completely to the Lord. By doing this, Moses made the entire tent and its furnishings holy for God's dwelling.

Moses sprinkled some of the anointing oil on the bronze altar of sacrifice seven times. He also anointed all its utensils, as well as the large water basin and its stand. Repeating the sprinkling seven times showed that the altar was made completely pure and ready for sacred service.

Moses poured the anointing oil generously over Aaron's head to consecrate him as high priest. While other items were only sprinkled, the oil was poured on Aaron so freely that it ran down his head and beard. This abundant pouring pictured the Holy Spirit being poured out without measure upon God's servants.

Moses brought Aaron's sons forward and clothed them in tunics, tied sashes around them, and placed headbands on their heads. These simpler white garments marked them as regular priests who would assist Aaron in the court. Moses followed the Lord's instructions to the letter.

Moses brought forward the bull for the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons pressed their hands hard upon its head. A sin offering was a sacrifice that took the penalty for guilt so the sinner could be forgiven. By pressing their hands on the animal, the priests symbolically passed their sins onto the innocent substitute.

Moses slaughtered the bull and used his finger to put some of its blood on the four raised corners of the altar. He poured the rest of the blood out at the base to purify the altar and prepare it for holy use. Atonement means covering sin and restoring a right relationship with God, and this blood cleansed the altar so sacrifices could be accepted there.

Moses collected all the fat covering the internal organs, the best part of the liver, and the two kidneys with their fat, and burned them on the altar. In Bible times, the fat was considered the richest and finest part of the animal. Burning it showed that the best portion of everything belongs to God alone.

Moses took the hide, meat, and dung of the bull and carried them outside the camp to burn them in the fire. In ordinary sin offerings the priests could keep the hide, but they were not allowed to benefit from an offering made for their own sins. Taking the remains outside the camp showed that their guilt was completely removed from the community.

Moses brought out the first ram, which was to be a burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. A burnt offering was a gift completely burned up to show total devotion and surrender to God. By laying their hands on the ram, the priests dedicated their whole lives to the Lord's service.

Moses killed the ram and sprinkled its blood against all four sides of the altar. The blood splashed around the altar marked it with the life of the sacrifice. This prepared the way for the entire animal to be offered to God.

Moses cut the ram into pieces, washed its inside parts and legs with clean water, and burned the entire animal on the altar. The whole ram was consumed by fire as a sweet-smelling gift that pleased the Lord. This showed that the priests were offering their complete devotion, inside and out, to God.

Moses brought out the second ram, called the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. This sacrifice was a peace offering that celebrated the priests entering into a close covenant with God. Their touch showed they were united with the sacrifice that brought them into fellowship with the Lord.

Moses slaughtered the ram and touched some of its blood to the tip of Aaron's right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot. The right side stood for a person's greatest strength and readiness to act. Blood on the ear meant listening to God's word, blood on the hand meant doing God's work, and blood on the foot meant walking in God's ways.

Moses brought Aaron's sons near and applied blood to their right earlobes, right thumbs, and right big toes as well. He then sprinkled the rest of the blood against the sides of the altar. This showed that the sons were also completely consecrated in what they heard, did, and how they lived.

Moses took the fat tail, the fat around the inner organs, the kidneys, the lobe of the liver, and the right thigh of the ram. From the basket of bread before the Lord, he also took one flat cake, one cake mixed with oil, and one wafer, placing them on top of the meat and fat. These portions formed the special ordination offering that would induct the priests into their sacred work.

Moses placed all these portions into the hands of Aaron and his sons and waved them before the Lord as a wave offering. The Hebrew term for ordaining priests literally means 'to fill the hands,' because giving them these gifts granted them the official right to handle God's sacrifices. Moving the offerings back and forth presented them directly to God.

Moses took the food back from the priests' hands and burned it all on the altar on top of the burnt offering. This ordination offering went up in smoke as a pleasant aroma to the Lord. Burning these gifts confirmed that the priests gave everything they received back to God in total surrender.

Moses took the breast of the ordination ram and waved it before the Lord as his own portion. Since Moses was acting as the officiating priest for this ceremony, God gave him the breast meat as his rightful share. Moses followed every detail just as the Lord had commanded.

Moses took anointing oil and blood from the altar and sprinkled them together on Aaron, his sons, and all their priestly garments. The blood showed they were cleansed by sacrifice, while the oil showed they were empowered by the Holy Spirit. Sprinkling both made the priests and their official clothes holy for the Lord's service.

Moses instructed Aaron and his sons to boil the remaining meat of the ram at the tabernacle entrance and eat it there with the holy bread. This sacred meal celebrated their new covenant of peace and fellowship with God. Any leftover food had to be burned with fire so that holy food would never spoil or be treated as ordinary.

Moses told Aaron and his sons not to leave the entrance of the Tent of Meeting for seven full days until their ordination was complete. In Scripture, seven represents fullness and perfection, showing that their preparation for holy service had to be thorough. Staying at the sanctuary kept them completely focused on God's work rather than worldly concerns.

Moses explained that the Lord had commanded everything done on this first day to be repeated to make atonement for them. These daily sacrifices showed that even the priests were ordinary sinners who needed ongoing forgiveness before they could represent others. True spiritual leaders must remember their own need for God's mercy.

Moses warned Aaron and his sons to stay at the tabernacle entrance day and night for seven days and obey God's charge so they would not die. Failing to keep God's commands in His holy presence brought the danger of death. This solemn warning reminded the priests of the awesome holiness of the God they served.

Aaron and his sons did everything the Lord commanded through Moses without changing a single detail. Their faithful obedience finished their ordination and set a righteous example for all Israel. They were now fully prepared to serve as mediators between God and His people.
